benefits: Straight-line distance between any two points, instantly.
Also gives the midpoint and the slope of the connecting line.

faqs.a: It is Pythagoras in disguise: the distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs |x2 - x1| and |y2 - y1|. So d = sqrt((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2).
faqs.q: Why does the formula use a square root?

faqs.a: Average the coordinates: ((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2). For (1, 2) and (4, 6) that is (2.5, 4).
A vertical line has undefined (infinite) slope because you would divide by zero. The tool says so honestly instead of showing a huge number.
faqs.q: Why does the slope say undefined?

faqs.a: No - this is the straight-line (Euclidean) distance on a flat plane. Road distances follow streets, and GPS distances follow the Earth's curve; both need different tools.
faqs.q: Is this the same as driving distance?

faqs.a: Yes. Decimals, negatives, and large values all work - the whole coordinate plane is supported.
The slope would be 0 / 0, which is meaningless. Distance is simply 0: the points are the same spot.
faqs.q: What if both points are identical?

distance-calculator.formula:
Distance: d = sqrt((x2 - x1) squared + (y2 - y1) squared)
Midpoint: ((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2)
Slope: m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
Example: (1, 2) to (4, 6): d = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5
howTo: Enter the x and y coordinates of point A.
Enter the x and y coordinates of point B.
The distance, midpoint, and slope appear instantly.
Decimals and negative coordinates are fully supported.
keyFacts: Distance = sqrt((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2) - the Pythagorean theorem.
A vertical line has undefined slope (division by zero).
Order of the points does not change the distance.

Slope is undefined for vertical lines (shown honestly as such).
Very large coordinates may lose a little floating-point precision.
